title: Getting solos with Lunceford; Hines let players grow
summary: Joining Lunceford made his name, since there was no featured trombonist; Hines had given him room to develop.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Of course, I left Earl and I went to New York to join Jimmy Lunceford, and this is when I really began to get a little name among the public because Jimmy was very popular with recordings in those days. And we did a lot of -- had a chance to play a lot of solos. I was very fortunate because he didn't have a trombone player prior to the time I came in there that did a lot of solo work. So, I got an opportunity to play a lot of solos. He had two good trombone players but they weren't really soloists, you know. They were more just good section men. So, I got -- It was a good break for me going with him because I got most all of the solos to do.
Had you been soloing a lot with Earl Hines?
Quite a bit. Quite extensively. Of course, Earl would feature most of the guys in the band.
I know you mentioned getting calls --
long distance calls about your broadcasts, (Inaudible).

Yeah. That's right. I mentioned that. But one thing about Earl, he would let you grow in his band. He'd give you a chance to, you know, to develop. And this was hard to find in most bands because you had to have it when you got there. They didn't give you a chance to develop. And Earl gave all of us this opportunity. So, I think it was a stroke of good fortune for me going with Earl, and also the timing was good for me going with Jimmy Lunceford because as soon as I got in Lunceford's band, as I mentioned to you earlier, I got a chance to do some solos that really helped me tremendously because "Margie" was the first thing I did, as I told you earlier, that really helped me, you know. And it was a very popular recording, so --
